title: FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS
body:
A directed readings course combining Fourier analysis with complex analysis, and the place where
most of the MATH block cashes out. The single idea underneath all of it: **any function can be
written as a sum of simple waves, and doing so turns hard operations into easy ones.** Differentiation
becomes multiplication, convolution becomes multiplication, and a differential equation becomes an
algebraic one. The course starts with periodic functions on an interval ([[Fourier Series]]), lets
the interval grow to the whole line ([[Fourier Transform]]), discretises so a computer can run it
([[Discrete Fourier Transform]]), and makes that run fast ([[Fast Fourier Transform]]). The second
half is complex analysis proper: integration along contours, the [[Residue Theorem]], and Evan's
final project on the [[Mandelbrot Set]].

It reaches further down the degree than any other MATH course. [[CALCULUS 2]] supplies the integrals
and the series-expansion idea, [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] and [[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]] supply the
projection-onto-a-basis argument that makes coefficients work at all, [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]]
supplies the PDEs that are the physical reason the series exists, and it pays back into
[[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]] (the theory behind the audio hardware),
[[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]] (the FFT as canonical divide and conquer), and
[[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] (the escape-time algorithm as a semi-decision procedure).

## Topics

### Fourier series

Decomposing a periodic function into sines and cosines, chapters 2 and 3 of the course.

- [[Fourier Series]] is the expansion itself, and the note carries the contrast with
  [[Taylor Series]]: both write a function as an infinite sum, one in powers and local, the other in
  sinusoids and global.
- [[Fourier Coefficients]] are the $a_0, a_n, b_n$, and each one is an integral that extracts a
  single frequency.
- [[Orthogonal Functions]] is why those integrals work: the sines and cosines are mutually
  orthogonal under $\int fg$, so each coefficient can be read off independently.
- [[Periodic Function]] sets the ground rules, fundamental period and piecewise continuity.
- [[Complex Exponential]] rewrites the whole thing in $e^{inx}$ via Euler's formula, collapsing two
  coefficient families into one.

### Convergence and behaviour

What the series does at the awkward points, and the conservation law it obeys.

- [[Gibbs Phenomenon]] is the roughly 9% overshoot at a jump discontinuity that never goes away no
  matter how many terms you add.
- [[Parseval's Identity]] says energy in the time domain equals energy in the frequency domain, which
  is Pythagoras on an [[Orthonormal Basis]] and the reason lossy compression works.

### The continuous transform

Chapter 4: the same decomposition for signals that never repeat.

- [[Fourier Transform]] takes the period to infinity, so the discrete list of frequencies becomes a
  continuous spectrum. The note carries the properties table: linearity, time shifting, modulation,
  scaling, and the derivative property.
- [[Convolution Theorem]] is the payoff. Convolution in one domain is pointwise multiplication in the
  other, which is why filtering, polynomial multiplication, and [[Image Processing]] kernels all
  route through the transform.

### Sampling: analog to digital

Chapter 5, and the bridge from continuous mathematics to anything a machine can store.

- [[Dirac Delta Function]] is the idealised impulse, and a train of them is the model of sampling.
- [[Sampling Theorem]] (Nyquist-Shannon) says a band-limited signal sampled above twice its highest
  frequency can be reconstructed **exactly**. This is why digital audio is possible.
- [[Aliasing]] is what undersampling does: a high frequency comes back as a clean low one that was
  never there, and the damage cannot be undone after the fact.

### The discrete transform

Chapter 6: finite data, finite sums, and the algorithm that made it practical.

- [[Discrete Fourier Transform]] replaces the integral with a sum over $N$ samples, which makes it
  [[Matrix Multiplication]] by the DFT matrix.
- [[Roots of Unity]] are the entries of that matrix, and they form a [[Cyclic Group]], one of the
  few places [[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]] visibly pays off elsewhere in the degree.
- [[Fast Fourier Transform]] exploits the roots' periodicity to get from $O(N^2)$ to $O(N \log N)$,
  by the same divide-and-conquer recurrence as [[Merge Sort]].

### Complex analysis

The second half of the directed reading.

- [[Complex Convergence]] does sequences, series, and the disc of convergence, and explains the
  puzzle [[Power Series]] leaves open: the radius is set by the nearest singularity in the plane,
  even when the function looks fine on the real line.
- [[Complex Integration]] is integration along a contour, structurally the [[Line Integral]] of
  [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]]. Cauchy's theorem kills every integral of an analytic function around a
  closed loop.
- [[Residue Theorem]] says a contour integral is $2\pi i$ times the sum of the enclosed residues,
  which evaluates real integrals that have no elementary antiderivative.

### Final project

- [[Mandelbrot Set]]: $z_{n+1} = z_n^2 + c$, the escape criterion at $|z| > 2$, and the fact that
  the algorithm can only ever *prove* a point is outside the set.
- [[Julia Set]] is the same iteration with $z_0$ and $c$ swapped, and the Mandelbrot set turns out to
  be the index of which Julia sets are connected.

## Core Facts to Know

- A [[Fourier Series]] writes a periodic function as $\frac{a_0}{2} + \sum(a_n\cos nx + b_n\sin nx)$.
- The coefficients are integrals, and they work because the basis functions are orthogonal:
  $\int_0^{2\pi}\cos(nx)\cos(mx)dx = 0$ unless $n = m$.
- A [[Fourier Coefficients|Fourier coefficient]] is a [[Projection]] onto a basis function. It is the
  [[Dot Product]] of [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] with the sum replaced by an integral.
- $\frac{a_0}{2}$ is the average value of the function. Even functions have no $b_n$; odd functions
  have no $a_n$.
- Euler's formula $e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta$ collapses the two coefficient families
  into one: $f \sim \sum c_n e^{inx}$.
- At a jump the series converges to the midpoint of the two one-sided limits, and overshoots by about
  9% on the way in. That overshoot is [[Gibbs Phenomenon]] and more terms do not remove it.
- [[Parseval's Identity]]: $\frac{1}{2\pi}\int|f|^2 = \sum|c_n|^2$. The transform moves information,
  it does not create or destroy it.
- The [[Fourier Transform]] is the series with the period taken to infinity: discrete coefficients
  become a continuous spectrum.
- Differentiation in time is multiplication by $2\pi i\xi$ in frequency. That is why the transform
  solves differential equations.
- **Squeeze in time and you stretch in frequency.** A [[Dirac Delta Function]] contains every
  frequency; a pure sine lasts forever.
- **[[Convolution Theorem]]: $\widehat{f * g} = \hat{f}\cdot\hat{g}$.** Convolution in one domain is
  multiplication in the other.
- [[Sampling Theorem]]: sample faster than **twice** the highest frequency present and the continuous
  signal is recoverable exactly. Slower, and [[Aliasing]] folds high frequencies down onto low ones
  irreversibly.
- Anti-aliasing filtering must happen **before** the sampler. After sampling it is too late.
- The [[Discrete Fourier Transform]] is $X_k = \sum_n x_n e^{-2\pi ikn/N}$, which is multiplication
  by the DFT matrix built from [[Roots of Unity]]. $N$ numbers in, $N$ numbers out.
- The DFT matrix rows are orthogonal, so the inverse transform is the conjugate transpose.
- Naive DFT is $O(N^2)$; the [[Fast Fourier Transform]] is $O(N\log N)$, from the recurrence
  $T(N) = 2T(N/2) + O(N)$. Same recurrence as [[Merge Sort]].
- FFT convolution beats direct convolution because $O(N\log N)$ beats $O(N^2)$: transform, multiply,
  transform back.
- A complex power series converges on a **disc**, and its radius is the distance to the nearest
  singularity in the plane.
- $\oint_\gamma f\,dz = 0$ when $f$ is analytic inside and on $\gamma$. All the value of a contour
  integral lives at the singularities.
- $\oint_{|z|=r} dz/z = 2\pi i$, and every other power integrates to zero. That is the whole reason
  residues are the $(z-z_0)^{-1}$ coefficient.
- [[Residue Theorem]]: $\oint_\gamma f\,dz = 2\pi i\sum\operatorname{Res}(f, z_k)$. For a simple pole,
  $\operatorname{Res} = \lim_{z\to z_0}(z - z_0)f(z)$.
- The [[Mandelbrot Set]] is the set of $c$ for which $z_{n+1} = z_n^2 + c$ from $z_0 = 0$ stays
  bounded. If $|z| > 2$ ever, it diverges.
- **Escaping is provable in finite time; staying bounded is not.** The black region of the picture is
  a guess at an iteration limit, which makes the set recognisable rather than decidable.
- $c$ is in the Mandelbrot set exactly when the [[Julia Set]] for that $c$ is connected.

## Related courses

- [[CALCULUS 2]] (MATH 2200) supplies both halves of the toolkit: [[Trigonometric Integrals]] and
  [[Integration By Parts]] evaluate the coefficient integrals, [[Infinite Series]] and
  [[Convergence Tests]] decide whether the expansion converges, and [[Taylor Series]] and
  [[Maclaurin Series]] are the same move in a different basis. [[Power Series]] asks the
  radius-of-convergence question that [[Complex Convergence]] answers.
- [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] (MATH 1203) supplies [[Complex Numbers]] and [[Polar Form]], which is where the
  [[Roots of Unity]] come from, plus the [[Vector Space]], [[Basis]], and [[Dot Product]] language
  that [[Orthogonal Functions]] generalises to infinitely many dimensions.
- [[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]] (MATH 2303) is the finite-dimensional rehearsal for this whole
  course. [[Inner Product]], [[Orthonormal Basis]], and [[Projection]] there are
  [[Fourier Coefficients]] here with the integral replaced by a sum. That course introduces the DFT
  as a change of basis on data and hands the transform itself to this one; it keeps
  [[Wavelet Transform]] and [[Image Processing]].
- [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]] (MATH 3200) is why the series exists physically. Separation of variables
  on the [[Heat Equation]] or the [[Wave Equation]] produces a family of modes, and fitting an
  initial condition to them is exactly a Fourier expansion. See
  [[Partial Differential Equations]]. [[Line Integral]], [[Parameterization]], and
  [[Green's Theorem]] are the real-variable rehearsal for [[Complex Integration]].
- [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]] (COMP 2659) built the hardware this course is the theory of. An
  [[DAC's and ADC's|ADC]] samples the waveform, [[Sampling Theorem]] says how fast it must;
  [[Fidelity]] degrades at low [[Sample Rate]], and [[Aliasing]] is the mechanism; [[PCM]] stores an
  [[Amplitude]] per sample, and the Dirac comb is the idealisation of that.
- [[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]] gets [[Fast Fourier Transform]] as a divide-and-conquer algorithm
  beside [[Merge Sort]], with the $O(N^2) \to O(N\log N)$ improvement stated in the language of
  [[Time Complexity]] and [[Asymptotic Analysis]].
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] (COMP 2613) is where the [[Mandelbrot Set]] lands: the escape-time
  algorithm is a semi-decision procedure, which is [[Undecidability]]'s distinction, and the
  simple-rule-to-complex-structure story is [[Cellular Automata]]'s.
- [[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]] (MATH 2101) supplies the [[Cyclic Group]] structure of the [[Roots of Unity]],
  the group the DFT matrix is built from.
- [[MACHINE LEARNING]] and [[Convolutional Neural Network]] are named for the operation
  [[Convolution Theorem]] defines. The kernels there are learned rather than designed, but the
  operation is the same one, and the frequency-domain view is why fast filtering is possible.

### 2.3 Fourier Series over Other Intervals

Our goal is to generalize a [[Fourier Series]] over an interval other than $[0,2\pi]$
We can do this by introducing a function $g(t)$ Where $t$ is defined by 
$$
\begin{matrix} \\
x \in [0, 2\pi]  \\
t \in [0, L]
\end{matrix}
$$
Where
$$
x = \frac{2\pi t}{L}
$$
The above [[Linear Transformation]] provides the following mappings
$$
\begin{align*}
t = 0 &\mapsto x = 0 \\
t = L &\mapsto x = 2\pi \\
\end{align*}
$$
Then we define $g(t) = f(x(t))$ such that 
$$
\begin{align*}
f(x) &\sim \frac{a_{0}}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left[a_{n}\cos\left(nx\right)+ b_{n}\sin\left(nx\right)\right] \\
\implies f(x(t)) = g(t) &\sim \frac{a_{0}}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left[a_{n}\cos\left(\frac{2n\pi t}{L}\right)+ b_{n}\sin\left(\frac{2n\pi t}{L}\right)\right] \\

\end{align*} 
$$
Now we have the series expansion for $g(t)$ over $t \in [0,L]$, now we need to find the [[Fourier Coefficients]]. 

Recall that 

$$
\begin{align*}
a_{n} = \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{2\pi}f(x)\cos(nx)dx \\
b_{n} = \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{2\pi}f(x)\sin(nx)dx
\end{align*}
$$
So we can use our substitution 
$$
\begin{align*}
x=\frac{2\pi t}{L} &\implies \frac{dx}{dt} = \frac{2\pi}{L} \\
&\implies dx = \frac{2\pi}{L}dt
\end{align*}
$$
Then we can find our coefficients by changing the bounds of integration and completing the substitution

$$
\begin{align*}
a_{n} &= \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{t=0}^{t=L}g(t)\cos\left(n\left(\frac{2\pi t}{L}\right)\right)\left(\frac{2\pi}{L}dt\right) \\
&= \frac{2\pi}{\pi L} \int_{t=0}^{t=L}g(t)\cos\left(\frac{2\pi nt}{L}\right)dt 
\end{align*}
$$
Likewise the $b_n$ coefficient can be found 
$$
b_{n}= \frac{2}{L} \int_{t=0}^{t=L}g(t)\sin\left(\frac{2\pi nt}{L}\right)dt
$$
